rationale: A wins because its proof discipline is sharper: it keeps asking for the missing customer, regulatory, and sourcing facts before letting the founder pretend this is bigger than the evidence. Its strongest line, "no named utility willing to say so," is a little too spicy, but it correctly treats the undisclosed customer as the wound in the story. B has good instincts, but "scheduled autonomous flights replace exactly the crewed inspection work an entire services layer sells" turns an unstated consequence into the angle. That is how a decent pitch becomes a reporter's skepticism package.
gaps_in_A: "A US drone maker bets the grid will pay a premium to avoid Chinese hardware" invents a price-premium premise. The update says US-made and positioned against Chinese makers, not that utilities will pay more.
"no named utility willing to say so" implies customer unwillingness. The fact supplied is narrower: no named utility is disclosed in the release.

"the first concrete evidence of where the 2024 exit led" is too absolute. The update says Skydio exited consumers two years ago and is launching this drone; it does not say there were no prior enterprise proof points.
gaps_in_B: "scheduled autonomous flights replace exactly the crewed inspection work an entire services layer sells" overclaims displacement. The update says no pilot, not that contractors lose work or contracts.
"utilities caught between Chinese hardware and import restrictions" is plausible but framed as a live squeeze without identifying the specific restrictions or current procurement pressure.

"first hard evidence of whether the two-year-old pivot produced a real enterprise product" is unsupported. The update does not establish that this is Skydio's first real enterprise product after the consumer exit.
"Next step: `journalist-fit-check`" is premature. Before shopping reporters, the founder needs a named utility, FAA/no-pilot detail, and proof of what the automated defect reports actually contain.
